d: Account takeover is when an attacker gains control of a legitimate user's online account, whether by stealing a password, forging a login token, or abusing a flaw that skips the login check. Once inside, they can read private data or act as the victim.
e: In August 2026, a critical Adobe Commerce flaw (CVE-2026-71362) allowed unauthenticated account takeover by letting an attacker switch their session to another shopper's account.

d: Active Directory Certificate Services — the built-in Microsoft Windows system that issues and manages the digital certificates used to prove identity inside a company network. Misconfigurations in AD CS are a common path attackers use to escalate from a normal account to full control of the domain.
e: The 'Certighost' exploit disclosed in July 2026 abused AD CS to let a low-privileged user obtain a Domain Controller certificate and take over the whole Active Directory domain.

d: A sophisticated, long-term cyberattack where an intruder gains network access and remains hidden for an extended period to steal data or cause damage.
e: A nation-state APT group silently accessed a defense contractor's network for 18 months, exfiltrating classified blueprints before detection.

d: Adversary-in-the-Middle (AitM) is a phishing technique where the attacker secretly relays traffic between the victim and the real website in real time. This lets them capture not just the password but also the session token that proves you are logged in, which is how AitM defeats many forms of multi-factor authentication.
e: In July 2026, the UNC6671 extortion crew used AitM tooling against Microsoft 365 and Okta logins to hijack hedge-fund employees' accounts despite MFA.

d: An AI system that plans and carries out long chains of actions on its own — running tools, reading results, deciding the next step — instead of answering one prompt at a time.
e: The Hugging Face intruder executed many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes with no human driving each step.

d: Restrictions built into a hosted AI model that make it refuse certain requests. Useful in general, but they can also block legitimate defensive work.
e: Hugging Face's forensic analysis was blocked by guardrails on the hosted models it first tried, while the attacker's model had no usage policy at all.

d: A defense that shuffles where a program's code and data sit in memory each time it runs, so an attacker who overflows a buffer cannot reliably predict where to jump. It turns many crashes into just crashes instead of takeovers.
e: F5 said the nginx CVE-2026-42533 overflow is a denial of service in normal conditions, but where ASLR is disabled or bypassed it may allow full remote code execution (July 2026).

d: The total sum of all points where an unauthorized user can try to enter or extract data from a system — including software, hardware, and human entry points.
e: A company's attack surface includes its website, employee email accounts, mobile apps, and cloud services.

d: How strongly researchers believe a named group is behind an attack. Reports are labeled low, moderate or high confidence, and low-confidence calls should be treated as a working hypothesis, not a fact.
e: Kaspersky tied the HelloNet ViPNet campaign to a Chinese-speaking APT with low confidence in July 2026 — the evidence was one unused string and a download mirror.

d: A flaw that lets an attacker skip the login check entirely instead of stealing or guessing a password. The system's own logic is broken, so it treats an unauthenticated stranger as a valid user.
e: In July 2026, ransomware affiliates exploited CVE-2026-0257 in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS to open GlobalProtect VPN sessions without any credentials, then deployed Qilin ransomware across victim networks.

d: Malware that quietly holds a door open for the attacker to return and run commands later, after the original way in has been closed or patched.
e: HelloExecutor and the Rust-based HelloBackdoor let the HelloNet operators run commands and move files long after the initial infection (July 2026).

d: A type of malware disguised as something legitimate that is built specifically to steal online banking credentials, session data, or funds once it infects a device. It often waits quietly until the victim opens a banking app or site before activating.
e: The Grandoreiro banking trojan resurfaced in a new campaign targeting bank customers across Latin America and Europe in August 2026.

d: A compulsory order issued by CISA that requires U.S. federal civilian agencies to take a specific security action, such as patching a dangerous flaw by a set deadline. Though only binding on federal agencies, BODs are widely treated as a signal that private organizations should act too.
e: In July 2026, CISA used BOD 26-04 to order federal agencies to patch the actively exploited Check Point SmartConsole flaw (CVE-2026-16232) by July 25.

d: A Baseboard Management Controller is a small always-on computer built into a server that lets admins power it on, reinstall the operating system, or mount media remotely, even when the main machine is off. Because it runs beneath the OS, malware there can survive a full disk wipe.
e: In August 2026 researchers found over 24,000 internet-exposed BMCs leaking password hashes through a 2013 IPMI flaw (CVE-2013-4786), letting attackers log in within minutes.

d: A network of private computers infected with malicious software and controlled as a group without the owners' knowledge, used to send spam or carry out attacks.
e: Hackers built a botnet of 500,000 infected home routers to launch a DDoS attack against a major bank's website.

d: A trial-and-error method to gain access by trying every possible combination of passwords or keys until the correct one is found, usually with automated tools.
e: Attackers used automated tools to try millions of password combinations per second against an online banking portal.

d: Short for Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver. An attacker installs a real, properly signed device driver that happens to contain a known flaw, then abuses that flaw to get deep kernel-level control of Windows and switch off security software. Windows loads it willingly because the signature is genuine.
e: In July 2026, Proofpoint documented the Cruciferra crypter dropping a legitimate but vulnerable driver called GoFlyDrv.sys and using its kernel access to find and terminate endpoint security processes before deploying remote access trojans.

d: Certified Third-Party Assessment Organization — the accredited outside auditor that performs CMMC Level 2 certification assessments.
e: There are 107 authorized C3PAOs against roughly 76,000 entities expected to need Level 2 certification.

d: The web page a public Wi-Fi network shows you before letting you online, usually asking you to accept terms or sign in. Because your device trusts this page, an attacker who controls it can redirect you to fake login or malware sites.
e: In July 2026, Russia's Midnight Blizzard tampered with hotel captive portals in its 'CaptiveCrunch' campaign to serve travelers fake Microsoft sign-in pages.

d: A certificate authority (CA) is the trusted system that issues digital certificates proving that a person, server, or computer is who it claims to be. If attackers can trick a CA into issuing certificates, they can impersonate trusted identities across a network.
e: In July 2026, the 'Certighost' flaw (CVE-2026-54121) let an ordinary domain user fool an enterprise Certificate Authority into issuing a certificate that impersonated a Domain Controller.

d: A CI/CD (continuous integration / continuous delivery) pipeline is the automated system that builds, tests and ships software. Compromising it lets attackers slip malicious code into everything the team releases.
e: The TeamCity CVE-2026-63077 flaw disclosed in August 2026 let attackers reach the build server and potentially poison the downstream CI/CD pipeline.

d: The U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency — issues alerts, advisories, and maintains the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog for critical infrastructure protection.
e: CISA issued an emergency directive requiring all federal agencies to patch a critical VPN vulnerability within 48 hours.

d: A social engineering technique where a fake error message or CAPTCHA page instructs the victim to copy and paste a command into their own computer, which silently installs malware. The victim performs the infection themselves.
e: A fake 'prove you're human' page told users to press Win+R and paste a command, which downloaded an information stealer — researchers found 3,000 live ClickFix payloads served by API-driven backends.

d: A clipboard hijacker (also called a 'clipper') is malware that watches whatever you copy and secretly swaps it before you paste — most often replacing a cryptocurrency wallet address with the attacker's so your payment goes to them. Because the switch happens invisibly at the moment of pasting, victims usually don't notice until the money is gone.
e: In July 2026, tampered Adform advertising code acted as a clipboard hijacker, replacing copied Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron addresses on any website that used Adform's tracking script.

d: The US Department of Defense/War programme that verifies defense contractors actually implement required cybersecurity controls, rather than just claiming to.
e: CMMC Phase 2 — the mandatory third-party audit stage — was suspended in July 2026 for a 60-day review.

d: A flaw where an application mistakes attacker-supplied data for its own instructions and runs it. If the injected input is executed as program code, the attacker can make the software do things it was never meant to do — often leading to full remote code execution.
e: The Langflow flaw CVE-2026-9198, added to CISA's KEV list in August 2026, was a code injection bug that let unauthenticated attackers run their own code on default installations.

d: The fundamental capability an exploit ultimately achieves — the "I can now run arbitrary code" moment. Multiple different exploit routes can reach the same primitive.
e: Two different gadget chains, same primitive: run code inside ServiceNow.

d: A flaw where an application passes attacker-supplied input straight into a command the underlying operating system runs, letting the attacker execute their own OS commands. It usually happens when a program builds a system command out of user input without safely separating data from instructions.
e: In July 2026, Arista's VeloCloud Orchestrator had a maximum-severity command injection flaw (CVE-2026-16812) that let unauthenticated attackers run any command on the server.

d: The infrastructure malware phones home to for instructions and to send stolen data out. Cutting C2 off usually neuters the malware.
e: The Hugging Face attacker used "self-migrating" C2 staged on public services, so blocking one address didn't stop it.

d: When an attacker breaks out of a container — a lightweight, isolated box that is supposed to keep an application separate from the host machine and its neighbors — and gains access to the underlying server. It turns a foothold in one confined app into control over everything running on that host.
e: In August 2026, Tencent researchers chained the 'SCTPhantom' Linux flaw (CVE-2026-64564) into a container escape, breaking out to gain root on the host operating system.

d: Reporting a flaw privately to the vendor, giving them time to patch, and publishing details only afterwards.
e: Searchlight Cyber reported the ServiceNow bug on 1 April 2026 and it was patched 13 July before details went public.

d: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, a US law that requires websites and apps to get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal data from children under 13. Violations are enforced by the FTC and Justice Department and can cost companies hundreds of millions of dollars.
e: In August 2026, TikTok agreed to pay $400 million to settle a Justice Department lawsuit alleging COPPA violations in how it handled children's accounts and data.

d: Invalidating existing keys, tokens and passwords and issuing new ones, so anything the attacker stole stops working.
e: Microsoft's advice on ACR Stealer stresses revoking session tokens, not just changing passwords — a stolen live token bypasses the new password entirely.

d: Credential stuffing is an attack where criminals take username-and-password pairs leaked from one breached site and automatically try them on many other sites, betting that people reuse passwords. It succeeds only because password reuse is so common.
e: In July 2026, Chick-fil-A disclosed a breach after attackers used credential stuffing to log into customer accounts with passwords stolen from unrelated sites.

d: Anything that proves identity to a system: passwords, API keys, access tokens, certificates. Stealing them is often more valuable than exploiting another bug.
e: Hugging Face users were told to rotate their access tokens because cloud and cluster credentials were stolen.

d: A web flaw where a site runs attacker-supplied code (usually JavaScript) because it displayed untrusted input without cleaning it first. The malicious code then runs in the victim's browser with the trust of that site.
e: In July 2026, the Russian group Laundry Bear exploited a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) bug in Microsoft Exchange OWA (CVE-2026-42897) so that merely viewing a crafted email ran their code.

d: Cryptographic agility means designing systems so the encryption algorithm can be swapped out without rewriting the whole application. It matters because algorithms eventually get broken and you need to be able to move fast when that happens.
e: In August 2026, the U.S. Treasury launched a Quantum-Readiness Task Force that named cryptographic agility as a core goal for financial firms preparing for post-quantum encryption.

d: An attack technique that hides malicious instructions inside encrypted or obfuscated content so security filters can't recognize them, only revealing the hidden commands once the target system decrypts or processes the content internally. It has been used to smuggle instructions past AI chatbot safety guardrails.
e: Researchers showed a Cryptographic Context Injection technique could bypass safety guardrails in both Grok and Gemini by hiding attacker instructions inside encrypted prompt content.

d: Cryptojacking is when an attacker secretly uses your computer or server to mine cryptocurrency for them, stealing your processing power and electricity. It rarely damages files - it just runs quietly in the background - so victims often only notice slow performance, heat, or high power bills.
e: In August 2026, attackers exploited a macOS Screen Sharing flaw (CVE-2026-65400) to gain root access and install a Monero cryptojacking miner on internet-exposed Macs.

d: Government information that isn't classified but still must be protected — technical drawings, contract data, personnel records.
e: Contractors handling CUI must still protect it under DFARS 252.204-7012 even though CMMC audits are paused.

d: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a publicly disclosed list of known cybersecurity vulnerabilities, each with a unique ID for consistent worldwide reference.
e: CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) was rated the most critical vulnerability of 2021 and affected millions of systems globally.

d: An organization officially authorized to assign CVE identifiers (the standard CVE-year-number IDs) to software flaws within a defined scope, such as its own products. CNAs are appointed and overseen by higher-level coordinators called Roots.
e: In August 2026, the NATO Cyber Security Centre and startup AISLE were onboarded as CVE Numbering Authorities under the ENISA Root, letting them issue CVE IDs for flaws in their scope.

d: Common Vulnerability Scoring System — rates the severity of security vulnerabilities on a scale of 0 to 10, where 10 is most critical. Helps organizations prioritize patching.
e: A CVSS score of 9.8 on a Microsoft Exchange vulnerability prompted emergency patching across thousands of organizations.

d: Distributed Denial of Service — an attack that floods a website or service with so much traffic from many sources that it becomes unavailable to legitimate users.
e: A DDoS attack knocked a major airline's booking website offline for six hours, causing millions in lost revenue.

d: The whole ecosystem of companies that supply the military — from prime contractors down to small subcontractors and machine shops.
e: The stated reason for pausing CMMC Phase 2 was that audit costs were pushing small firms out of the DIB.

d: An attack or bug that makes a system crash, hang, or stop responding so legitimate users can't reach it. It does not steal data, but it can take a service offline.
e: Citrix first described the NetScaler flaw CVE-2026-8452 in 2026 as a Denial of Service memory bug before researchers showed it could also be pushed to full remote code execution.

d: Making a system unavailable rather than stealing from it — by crashing it or exhausting its memory, CPU or bandwidth.
e: The OpenSSL "HollowByte" flaw makes a server reserve up to 131 KB of memory for a message that never arrives, using an 11-byte request.

d: The process of turning stored or transmitted data back into objects a program can use. When software deserializes untrusted data without checks, attackers can smuggle in malicious code that executes during the rebuild.
e: CISA added a SharePoint deserialization flaw to its KEV catalog after attackers used crafted data packets to run their own code on unpatched servers.

d: A phishing technique that abuses the OAuth 'device code' sign-in flow (built for TVs and gadgets that can't show a login page). The attacker starts a real login and tricks you into approving it on the genuine site, so no password is stolen and MFA is satisfied for real.
e: In August 2026 Dark Reading reported device code phishing rose about 1,500% in the first half of 2026, with attackers approving their own logins via victims' legitimate Microsoft sign-ins.

d: The contract clause that legally obliges defense contractors to implement NIST SP 800-171 and report cyber incidents. It sits in the contract itself, independent of CMMC.
e: The CMMC pause changed nothing about this clause — it's still in every affected contract.

d: Examining logs, memory and disk images to reconstruct exactly what an attacker did, when, and what they took.
e: Hugging Face brought in external forensic experts and found its AI tooling's guardrails obstructed the analysis.

d: A European Union competition law that limits how the largest tech 'gatekeeper' platforms operate, for example barring them from unfairly favouring their own services over rivals'.
e: In July 2026, the EU issued its first DMA fine, penalising Google €890 million for self-preferencing in search and restricting app developers in the Play Store.

d: Planting a malicious DLL (a Windows code library) next to a trusted program so that when the trusted program starts, Windows loads the attacker's library instead of the real one. The malware inherits the trusted program's reputation and privileges.
e: HelloNet dropped a fake wtsapi32.dll into the ViPNet update folder so the legitimate itcsrvup64.exe loaded it at every boot (July 2026).

d: DNS rebinding is a trick where a malicious website makes your browser connect to a device or service on your own private network instead of the internet. It abuses how browsers trust a domain name, letting an outside attacker reach 'internal-only' systems that have no public login.
e: In August 2026, CISA added a Ray AI-framework flaw (CVE-2025-62593) to its KEV catalog partly because it could be triggered via DNS rebinding straight from a victim's web browser.

d: A ransomware tactic where attackers steal a copy of your data before encrypting it, then threaten to publish the stolen copy as well as keep your files locked. Restoring from backup no longer ends the problem.
e: In July 2026, Arctic Wolf reported Qilin operators using Rclone to copy victim data to MEGA cloud storage before encryption, so victims with good backups still faced a leak threat.

d: A memory bug where a program releases (frees) the same block of memory twice. Attackers can exploit the resulting corruption to crash the program or run their own code with the program's privileges.
e: In August 2026, CISA added CVE-2026-33824, a Double Free flaw in the Windows IKE service, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after attackers used it for remote code execution.

d: Executable and Linkable Format — the standard file format for programs on Linux and Unix, the equivalent of a .exe on Windows. Finding an unexpected ELF file on an appliance is a strong sign of compromise.
e: UTA0533 wrote an ELF executable named /usr/bin/xzfind onto a SonicWall SMA appliance on 22 June 2026.

d: The process of converting readable data into an unreadable format using an algorithm, so only authorized parties with the correct decryption key can access it.
e: Your bank uses end-to-end encryption so intercepted transaction data cannot be read by attackers.

d: Entropy is the amount of true randomness available when generating secret keys or passwords. Low entropy means the output is predictable, so an attacker can guess it.
e: In August 2026, a weak random-number function in CryptoJS produced low-entropy recovery phrases, letting thieves drain about $5.7 million from five crypto wallet apps.

d: EtherNet/IP is a common industrial networking protocol that control equipment such as PLCs uses to talk to workstations and other systems over standard Ethernet. It was designed for trusted factory networks and generally has no built-in authentication, so exposing it to the internet is dangerous.
e: In August 2026, thousands of water-system controllers were found reachable over the public internet via EtherNet/IP, letting outsiders potentially read or change their configuration.

d: A piece of software, code, or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability in a system to cause unintended behavior — usually to gain unauthorized access.
e: Hackers developed an exploit for an unpatched Windows vulnerability allowing full remote control of any affected machine.

d: Combining two or more flaws so that the output of one enables the next, reaching an impact neither could achieve alone.
e: Wp2shell chains a REST API routing bug with a SQL injection to get from anonymous request to code execution.

d: A US law making it fraud to submit false claims to the government. Under DOJ's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative it's applied to contractors who misrepresent their security posture.
e: MORSE Corp paid $4.6M over the gap between its self-reported score and what assessors actually found.

d: Deliberately leaving clues that point at someone else — a foreign language string, another group's tooling — so investigators blame the wrong party.
e: Kaspersky explicitly kept a false flag on the table when tentatively attributing HelloNet to a Chinese-speaking group in July 2026.

d: Running malicious code entirely in RAM without writing it to disk, so file-scanning antivirus has nothing to find and a reboot erases the evidence.
e: HelloInjector ran its HelloProxy payload in memory; separately, the second compromised SonicWall appliance lost its memory-resident backdoors when it was rebooted on 2 July 2026.

d: A network security device that monitors and controls incoming/outgoing network traffic based on security rules — acts as a barrier between trusted and untrusted networks.
e: A hospital firewall blocked thousands of unauthorized connection attempts per day from external IP addresses.

d: A vendor mechanism that pushes a security fix to installations automatically, without waiting for the owner to act. Effective, but only for installs that haven't disabled it.
e: WordPress used forced auto-updates to push 6.9.5 / 7.0.2 for wp2shell; self-managed sites with auto-update off are the exposed tail.

d: A small piece of existing, legitimate code that an attacker strings together with others to build an exploit — like assembling a weapon from spare parts already lying around.
e: Attackers reached ServiceNow code execution via a different sandbox-escape gadget than the researchers' published one, so signature-based blocks on the original PoC miss it.

d: The Government Accountability Office is a nonpartisan U.S. federal watchdog agency that investigates how government agencies spend money and use their authority, then reports its findings to Congress. It has no enforcement power itself, but its reports often shape future oversight and legislation.
e: In August 2026, lawmakers asked the GAO to review how federal agencies use spyware and other hacking tools against Americans.

d: General Data Protection Regulation — EU law governing how organizations collect, store, and use personal data. Violations can result in fines up to 4% of global annual revenue.
e: A U.S. company was fined €20 million under GDPR for failing to secure European customer data exposed in a breach.

d: An attack that hides malicious instructions inside data an AI agent will later read (such as firewall logs), so the organization's own AI agent unknowingly carries out the attacker's commands. It is a specific twist on prompt injection aimed at agents wired into real infrastructure.
e: At DEF CON in August 2026, researchers used Ghostjacking to hide commands in Cloudflare firewall logs and hijacked an AI coding agent nine times out of ten.

d: A query language and API style that lets an app request exactly the data it needs from a single flexible endpoint, instead of many fixed URLs. Because one endpoint exposes a lot of functionality, a bug in it can have wide reach.
e: In August 2026, a code-injection flaw in a GitLab GraphQL directive (CVE-2026-19478) let unauthenticated attackers modify or delete public projects.

d: Hacking back means going on the offensive against an attacker's own systems - for example to disrupt or destroy their infrastructure - rather than only defending your own network. It is legally restricted for private companies in most countries because of the risk of hitting the wrong target.
e: In August 2026, a White House memo proposed letting vetted U.S. security firms hack back against foreign cybercrime gangs under government oversight.

d: Writing more data into a memory area than was reserved for it, corrupting adjacent memory. Can crash a process or, in the worst case, be steered into code execution.
e: Nginx CVE-2026-42533 lets a crafted HTTP request overflow a worker-process buffer, causing denial of service and potentially RCE.

d: The U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a law setting rules for protecting patients' health information. It requires healthcare organizations and their contractors to safeguard that data and to notify regulators and affected people when a breach occurs.
e: In July 2026, medical-billing firm MCBS reported a HIPAA breach to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services affecting over 1.26 million people.

d: A decoy system deliberately left exposed to attract attackers so defenders can watch how they operate and detect new attacks early. It has no real business use, so any interaction with it is suspicious by definition.
e: In August 2026, WatchTowr's honeypot sensors caught the first in-the-wild exploitation of the critical GitLab flaw about two days after it was disclosed.

d: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the system that decides who a user is and what they are allowed to do -- handling logins, permissions, and access to apps and data.
e: In August 2026, Microsoft's Entra ID, a cloud IAM service, had a maximum-severity flaw (CVE-2026-69836) that let unauthenticated attackers run code remotely.

d: Industrial Control Systems / Operational Technology — computer systems controlling physical industrial processes like power grids and water treatment. Cyberattacks can cause real-world physical damage.
e: A cyberattack on a water treatment plant's ICS briefly altered chemical levels in the water supply.

d: A flaw where a system fails to correctly verify who a user really is, letting an attacker access it without valid credentials. It is a common cause of account takeover and unauthorized access.
e: In August 2026, Apple macOS flaw CVE-2026-65400 (CVSS 9.8) let an attacker on the network log into Screen Sharing with no valid password due to Improper Authentication.

d: Confirmation that real attackers are using a flaw against real targets right now — as opposed to it existing only in a lab or a research paper.
e: Defused observed live attack traffic against ServiceNow instances, which is what moved CVE-2026-6875 from "theoretical" to "drop everything".

d: The organised process of detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from an attack — and working out what happened.
e: Volexity discovered UTA0533 while running an IR engagement at a victim organization.

d: A type of malware designed to quietly harvest sensitive data from an infected device, such as saved passwords, browser cookies, and authentication tokens, and send it back to an attacker.
e: Microsoft warned that a surge in ACR Stealer infections was letting attackers harvest browser-stored passwords and login tokens from enterprise customers.

d: An initial access broker is a criminal who breaks into company networks and then sells that foothold to other attackers, such as ransomware crews, instead of doing the final attack themselves.
e: In August 2026, the sentenced Ransom Cartel operator was described as working with initial access brokers who supplied ready-made access to victim corporate networks.

d: Indicators of Compromise — evidence a system has been breached, such as suspicious IP addresses, unusual file hashes, or abnormal network traffic patterns used to detect and investigate attacks.
e: Analysts identified IOCs including a known malicious IP and a suspicious file appearing on 40 company machines.

d: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, digitally signed piece of data a server issues to prove who a user is and what they are allowed to do, so the user does not have to log in again on every request. If the signature checking is flawed, an attacker can forge a token and impersonate someone.
e: In August 2026, attackers exploited SharePoint flaw CVE-2026-55040 by forging a JWT that declared no signature was needed, letting them log in as any user.

d: Known Exploited Vulnerabilities — CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities actively being exploited in the wild. Federal agencies must patch KEV entries within strict deadlines.
e: CISA added a critical Cisco IOS vulnerability to its KEV catalog, giving federal agencies 72 hours to patch.

d: Moving sideways from the first compromised machine to other systems inside the same network, usually using stolen credentials.
e: After stealing cloud and cluster keys from one worker node, the Hugging Face attacker moved laterally across several internal clusters.

d: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol — the protocol corporate systems use to check usernames and passwords against a central directory such as Active Directory. If it travels unencrypted, anyone watching the wire sees the logins.
e: On a compromised SonicWall appliance, UTA0533 ran tcpdump against unencrypted LDAP traffic to harvest usernames and passwords (July 2026).

d: Living off the land is when attackers avoid installing obvious malware and instead abuse legitimate, already-trusted tools and services to carry out their attack. Because the activity looks normal, it is much harder for defenders to spot.
e: In August 2026, the TWINLOOT Python implant hid all of its command-and-control traffic inside trusted Microsoft SharePoint and Teams, a textbook living-off-the-land technique.

d: A load balancer is a device or service that spreads incoming network traffic across multiple servers so no single server gets overwhelmed. Because it sits at the network edge and inspects traffic, a flaw in one can hand attackers a foothold into the network.
e: In August 2026, CISA flagged CVE-2026-8037, a command-injection bug in the Progress Kemp LoadMaster load balancer, as actively exploited.

d: Small, simple malware whose only job is to get a foothold and then pull down the real tools. Keeping stage one tiny makes it harder to detect and lets the attacker swap what comes next.
e: HelloInjector did nothing but inject into svchost.exe and fetch further modules from the C2 (July 2026).

d: A machine key is a secret value a web server (such as SharePoint or ASP.NET) uses to sign and encrypt the authentication tokens and cookies it hands out, so it can trust them later. If an attacker steals it, they can forge tokens the server will accept as genuine, even after a patch.
e: In July 2026, attackers exploited a SharePoint flaw (CVE-2026-50522) to steal machine keys, letting them forge valid logins even after the server was patched.

d: Malvertising is the practice of spreading malware through online advertisements, sometimes even on legitimate, well-known websites. Simply loading a page that contains a poisoned ad can be enough to put a user at risk, without them ever clicking anything unusual.
e: In July 2026, a malvertising campaign called 'SourTrade' impersonated TradingView and other finance brands to trick crypto investors across 12 countries into downloading a browser-assembled Windows trojan.

d: Short for malicious software — any software intentionally designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorized access to a system. Includes viruses, ransomware, spyware, and trojans.
e: Employees unknowingly installed malware disguised as a shipping notification attachment, granting attackers full network access.

d: A criminal business model where one group builds malware and rents it out to other criminals, much like a legitimate software subscription. It lets low-skill attackers launch sophisticated attacks they could never write themselves.
e: In July 2026, the Golden Chickens MaaS operation (aka Venom Spider) resurfaced with four new rentable malware families including TinyEgg and ChonkyChicken.

d: Multi-Factor Authentication — requires users to verify identity using two or more factors: something you know (password), have (phone), or are (fingerprint). Dramatically reduces account takeover risk.
e: Even after attackers obtained an employee's password from the dark web, MFA prevented system access.

d: An open standard that lets AI assistants and agents plug into external tools, data sources, and services in a consistent way. It expands what an AI can do, but each connected tool is code the AI is trusting.
e: In August 2026, researchers showed a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could split a harmful request into innocent-looking steps to make an AI coding agent leak SSH keys and secrets.

d: An N-day is a vulnerability that has already been publicly disclosed and has a patch available - the opposite of a zero-day. Attackers love them because plenty of organizations take weeks or years to apply fixes.
e: In August 2026, an NSA and FBI advisory said the China-nexus group QTFY used both zero-day and N-day flaws, including a 2024 Check Point bug (CVE-2024-24919) that had been patched for over a year.

d: National Institute of Standards and Technology — develops cybersecurity standards and frameworks, most notably the NIST CSF, with five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
e: After a breach, a healthcare company used the NIST CSF to redesign its entire security program.

d: The NIST publication listing 110 security requirements for protecting CUI on non-federal systems. It defines the "what"; CMMC defines how it's verified.
e: A contractor reporting a perfect score claims all 110 controls are fully implemented.

d: OAuth is the technology behind 'Sign in with Google/Microsoft' buttons: it lets one app access your account by issuing it a limited access token, so the app never sees your actual password.
e: In August 2026, suspected Russian hackers routed defense-sector targets through a genuine Google OAuth consent screen and then stole the resulting access tokens to hijack their accounts.

d: The specialized computers, controllers and sensors that run physical equipment like pumps, valves and factory machines, as opposed to the regular IT that runs email and office apps. Attacks on it can have real-world physical effects.
e: In July 2026, cyberattacks on the operational technology behind U.S. water utilities in seven states forced several plants to switch to manual control.

d: A phishing-resistant replacement for passwords that uses a private key stored on your device instead of a secret you type in. The website only ever sees a public key, so there is no password for an attacker to steal or trick you into revealing.
e: In August 2026 Unit 42's 'Pass-ta-key' research showed that malware already on a PC could hijack Google-synced passkeys without breaking the underlying passkey cryptography.

d: An attack that tries a few commonly used passwords across a huge number of accounts, instead of many passwords against one account. It stays under account-lockout limits, making it hard to detect.
e: A campaign against Microsoft's Azure CLI generated 81 million login attempts in two weeks by spraying common passwords across thousands of tenants, compromising at least 78 accounts.

d: A software update released by a vendor to fix a security vulnerability or bug. Applying patches promptly is one of the most effective ways to prevent cyberattacks.
e: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday released fixes for 87 vulnerabilities, including three already exploited in the wild.

d: A patch bypass is when researchers or attackers find a way around a fix a vendor already shipped, so the vulnerability is exploitable again even on 'patched' systems. It usually happens because the first fix blocked one specific attack path instead of the underlying flaw.
e: In August 2026, watchTowr and Huntress defeated PaperCut's first emergency patch for two actively exploited NG/MF flaws, forcing the vendor to publish Emergency Patch Release 2 on August 28.

d: The second Tuesday of each month, when Microsoft (and some other vendors) release their scheduled bundle of security updates. Grouping fixes on a predictable day helps IT teams plan testing and deployment.
e: On August 2026 Patch Tuesday, Microsoft fixed roughly 400 vulnerabilities, including a Windows afd.sys zero-day already exploited by North Korean hackers.

d: Tricking a program into reading or writing a file outside the folder it was supposed to stay in, usually by smuggling ../ sequences into a filename.
e: CVE-2026-15410 is a path traversal in SonicWall's remove_hotfix workflow — the step that turned non-root access into root (July 2026).

d: Anything an attacker sets up so their access survives a reboot or a password change — a modified startup script, a scheduled task, a new service.
e: UTA0533 edited /etc/init.d/workplace so its web shell relaunched every time the SonicWall appliance restarted (July 2026).

d: A cyberattack using deceptive emails or messages appearing to come from trusted sources, tricking recipients into revealing sensitive information or clicking malicious links.
e: Emails mimicking the company's IT department captured 200 employee passwords in a single day.

d: Phishing-as-a-Service is a criminal business model that rents ready-made phishing kits, fake login pages, and hosting to other crooks, so even unskilled attackers can run convincing campaigns. It works like a subscription software product, but for fraud.
e: In July 2026, police dismantled Kratos, a phishing-as-a-service platform whose roughly 1,800 customers ran about 15,000 phishing campaigns a month.

d: A cloud model where the provider runs the servers and platform, and customers build applications and workflows on top of it.
e: ServiceNow AI Platform is a PaaS product running 100+ billion workflows a year.

d: A Windows feature that automatically detects newly connected hardware and installs the driver or helper software it needs, with no manual setup by the user. Convenient, but it means the operating system will fetch and run vendor code on your behalf.
e: In August 2026, researchers abused Windows Plug and Play in the 'Plug And Pwn' technique, making Windows 11 auto-install signed vendor software they then chained into full SYSTEM access.

d: Post-quantum cryptography is a set of new encryption methods designed to stay secure even against future quantum computers, which could break much of today's encryption. Organizations are beginning to adopt it now because data stolen today could be decrypted later once quantum machines mature.
e: In August 2026, Google Cloud published a roadmap to be ready for post-quantum cryptography by 2029.

d: Exploitable without any username, password or session — the attacker doesn't need an account. Dramatically worse than a bug requiring a valid login.
e: CVE-2026-6875 is a "pre-auth sandbox-escape RCE" — a total stranger on the internet can reach it.

d: Turning limited access into powerful access — e.g. a normal user account becoming an administrator.
e: Many of the flaws in the July 2026 Microsoft Patch Tuesday were elevation-of-privilege bugs that let a low-level foothold become domain admin.

d: A PRNG (pseudorandom number generator) is a formula that produces numbers that look random but are actually calculated from a starting value called a seed. If the seed is guessable or the generator is weak, an attacker can reproduce the exact same 'random' numbers — catastrophic when those numbers are used to create secret keys.
e: In July 2026, a weak PRNG in Coldcard hardware-wallet firmware let attackers reproduce users' wallet seeds and steal an estimated $88.6 million in Bitcoin.

d: A Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) is a small, rugged industrial computer that directly runs physical equipment like pumps, valves, and motors in factories and utilities. Because it controls real-world machinery, a compromised PLC can cause physical damage, not just data loss.
e: In August 2026, researchers found over 4,400 Rockwell PLCs exposed directly to the internet, including some in U.S. cities whose water systems had already been attacked.

d: An attack against an AI system where hidden or malicious text tricks the model into ignoring its instructions and taking unintended actions, such as leaking data or running commands.
e: A single crafted prompt let attackers escape an AI code editor's safety sandbox and execute commands, with no click or approval needed from the victim.

d: Sample code or a demonstration that researchers publish to prove a vulnerability is real and exploitable, usually shared so defenders can verify and patch it.
e: Attackers hid a password-stealing trojan inside a fake proof-of-concept exploit posted to GitHub, targeting researchers who ran it to test the claimed vulnerability.

d: A tool planted on a compromised internet-facing server that relays the attacker's traffic onward into the internal network, disguised as ordinary web requests to that server.
e: UTA0533 injected Suo5, an open-source HTTP proxy, into a legitimate SonicWall process and reached it at /workplace/error.jsp (July 2026).

d: The anticipated future date when quantum computers become powerful enough to break the public-key encryption that protects today's internet traffic, banking, and government secrets. Nobody knows exactly when it will arrive, so migration to quantum-resistant algorithms is happening years in advance.
e: In August 2026, US senators introduced the Quantum-GUARD Act to prepare the electric grid for Q-Day by pushing utilities toward post-quantum cryptography.

d: A modern internet transport protocol, used by HTTP/3, that runs over UDP and encrypts nearly everything to make connections faster and more private than classic TCP. That same heavy encryption makes malicious traffic hidden inside QUIC hard for security tools to inspect.
e: In August 2026, the QUICAgent backdoor from Operation QUICSILVER hid its command-and-control traffic inside QUIC connections while spying on Myanmar government targets.

d: A timing flaw where two operations run at nearly the same moment and an attacker exploits the tiny gap between them to change data or bypass a check before the system finishes its work.
e: In July 2026, the RefluXFS Linux flaw (CVE-2026-64600) used a race condition in the XFS filesystem to let a normal user overwrite root-owned files and take over the machine.

d: Malware that encrypts a victim's files, making them inaccessible, then demands payment (usually cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key to restore access.
e: A hospital chain paid a $4.5M ransom after ransomware encrypted records across 50 facilities, halting surgeries.

d: A criminal business model where one group builds the ransomware and rents it to other criminals (called affiliates) who carry out the actual attacks, then split the ransom. It lets people with little technical skill run damaging attacks.
e: In August 2026 a joint government advisory described Gunra as a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation whose affiliates had hit at least 51 healthcare, finance, and government organizations.

d: A criminal business model in which the developers who build ransomware rent it out to other attackers ('affiliates'), who carry out the break-ins and split the ransom profits. It lets people with little technical skill launch sophisticated ransomware attacks.
e: The DevMan RaaS operation detailed in July 2026 ran a web portal where affiliates could build their own ransomware payloads and track their earnings.

d: The attacker's look-around phase after getting in: what machine is this, who is logged on, what else is reachable. It usually precedes the damaging part.
e: HelloExecutor's job in the HelloNet campaign was command execution and network reconnaissance on the infected host (July 2026).

d: Malware that gives an attacker hands-on remote control of an infected computer, letting them run commands, steal files, or watch activity as if they were sitting at the keyboard.
e: In July 2026, the Chaos ransomware gang deployed a Rust RAT called msaRAT that hid its remote-control traffic inside a headless Chrome browser to avoid detection.

d: A vulnerability that lets an attacker run their own commands or programs on a victim's device or server from across a network, often without needing a password.
e: A pre-authentication RCE flaw in a load balancer let attackers run arbitrary commands on the device without ever logging in.

d: A standard machine-to-machine web interface: programs send structured HTTP requests to defined "routes" (URLs) instead of clicking through pages.
e: WordPress's REST API batch route could be confused about which internal handler should process a request — the first half of wp2shell.

d: A server that sits between users and a real website, forwarding traffic in both directions. Legitimate ones balance load and add security, but attackers use malicious reverse proxies to silently relay a victim's login to the real site while capturing everything typed.
e: In August 2026, the Mirage2FA phishing service used an adversary-in-the-middle reverse proxy to relay victims' Microsoft 365 logins in real time, capturing credentials and session cookies together.

d: A reverse shell is a trick where the victim's machine opens a connection out to the attacker, giving the attacker a command line on that machine. It is popular because firewalls usually block incoming connections but allow outgoing ones, so the outbound 'call home' slips through.
e: In August 2026, an APT exploiting the VMware vCenter flaw CVE-2026-59310 dropped the open-source reverse_ssh tool to keep a reverse shell open on compromised servers.

d: Remote Monitoring and Management — software that IT teams and managed service providers use to watch, control, and push updates to many computers remotely from one console. Because a single RMM server has trusted access to every machine it manages, attackers prize it as a way to reach hundreds of systems at once.
e: In August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18577) in the N-able N-central RMM platform and abused its remote-access feature to pivot into customers' managed endpoints.

d: The all-powerful administrator account on Unix/Linux systems (Windows equivalent: SYSTEM or Administrator). Root can read, change, or hide anything.
e: The chained SonicWall flaws give the attacker root on the VPN appliance — complete ownership of the box.

d: Malicious software designed to hide deep in a computer and give an attacker stealthy, high-level control while evading detection. "Kernel-mode" rootkits run in the operating system's core, making them especially hard to spot or remove.
e: In August 2026, North Korean hackers exploited a Windows WinSock zero-day (CVE-2026-68820) to install a kernel-mode rootkit for persistent SYSTEM-level control.

d: A restricted environment where untrusted code is allowed to run but is walled off from the rest of the system.
e: ServiceNow runs customer scripts in a sandbox; CVE-2026-6875 is a "sandbox escape" — breaking out of that wall.

d: A flaw that lets code break out of the restricted area it was supposed to be confined to and run on the underlying system. Sandboxes exist so that untrusted code can run safely; an escape means the wall did not hold.
e: In July 2026, the automation platform n8n patched an 8.7-rated sandbox escape that allowed anyone with permission to edit a workflow to run operating-system commands as the n8n process itself.

d: Short for Software Bill of Materials: a machine-readable ingredients list of every component and library inside a piece of software. It lets defenders instantly check whether they are affected when a new vulnerability appears.
e: In July 2026, CISA, the NSA, and the FBI released updated '2026 Minimum Elements for an SBOM' guidance adding required fields like component hashes and licenses.

d: Short for Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition: software and hardware that monitor and control physical industrial equipment such as power grids, water systems, and factory machinery. A flaw here can have real-world safety consequences, not just data loss.
e: In August 2026, CVE-2026-25895 in the FUXA SCADA/HMI platform let unauthenticated attackers write files and run code on systems controlling industrial equipment.

d: Software-Defined Wide Area Network: technology that uses software to intelligently route traffic across multiple internet or private links connecting an organization's offices, instead of relying on fixed hardware routing. A central controller manages all the sites, which makes that controller a high-value target.
e: In July 2026, a flaw in Arista's VeloCloud SD-WAN controller could have handed attackers control of every branch-office device it managed.

d: A list of (usually 12 or 24) ordinary words that is the master key to a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone who obtains the seed phrase can take full control of the funds, so it must never be stored where software can read it.
e: In August 2026, malicious "Solidity Pro" VS Code extensions searched developers' machines for wallet seed phrases and stole them over Telegram.

d: A flaw that tricks a server into making network requests chosen by the attacker, often reaching internal systems the attacker could not contact directly. It is frequently chained with other bugs to break deeper into a network.
e: In 2026, SonicWall SMA1000 CVE-2026-15409, a CVSS 10 server-side request forgery bug, was chained with a code-injection flaw to gain root access.

d: A flaw that tricks a server into making network requests chosen by the attacker. Because the request comes from the trusted server, it can reach internal systems the attacker could never contact directly.
e: In July 2026, CVE-2026-15409 in SonicWall SMA1000 appliances — rated CVSS 10.0 — let unauthenticated attackers force the appliance to send requests to unintended internal locations.

d: A small token your browser stores after you log in, proving to the website that you're already authenticated so you don't have to re-enter your password on every page. If an attacker steals it, they can impersonate you without knowing your password or passing MFA.
e: In August 2026, the Mirage2FA phishing kit stole authenticated Microsoft 365 session cookies from roughly 4,500 companies, letting attackers walk straight into accounts despite two-factor authentication.

d: An attack where someone steals the session token (the cookie your browser keeps after you log in) so they are treated as already signed in, without ever needing your password. Because the login already happened, it can slip past multi-factor authentication.
e: In August 2026 Anthropic warned that infostealer malware was hijacking users' Claude sessions and draining their paid usage after stealing the login cookies from infected PCs.

d: A Unix program flagged to run with its owner's privileges rather than the privileges of whoever launched it. A setuid-root program run by a low-privilege user executes as root — which is exactly why attackers plant their own.
e: ROOTRUN, the ELF file UTA0533 dropped as /usr/bin/xzfind, was a setuid binary that let an unprivileged account run any command as root (July 2026).

d: A form of blackmail where an attacker threatens to share sexual images or messages of a victim unless they pay money or provide more content. It frequently targets teenagers and children.
e: In August 2026 a member of the cybercrime group The Com was sentenced to two years in prison for sextortion against nearly 120 victims worldwide.

d: AI tools that employees use for work without approval or oversight from their IT or security team, creating blind spots for data protection and compliance. A stricter cousin, 'Shady AI', is when approved tools are used in unapproved or poorly governed ways.
e: In a July 2026 SANS survey, 76% of security teams said they now have a formal role in governing enterprise AI, largely to rein in Shadow AI.

d: In application security, the dangerous end-point where attacker-controlled data finally gets used — e.g. passed to a code evaluator or a database query. The entry point is the "source".
e: Attackers targeted the same pre-auth sink (/assessment_thanks.do) that the original researchers documented.

d: A small program stored on a blockchain that automatically runs and returns data when called. Because blockchain data is public and cannot be edited or deleted, criminals sometimes abuse smart contracts to store information that is hard for police to take down.
e: In August 2026, the DeadLock ransomware group used Polygon smart contracts to store its command-and-control address so defenders could not seize a single server to disrupt it.

d: Simple Network Management Protocol — a standard language that servers, routers, and printers use to report their status and accept monitoring commands over a network. SNMP services often run with high privileges, so a flaw in one can hand an attacker control of the entire device.
e: In August 2026, CISA ordered federal agencies to patch a Zimbra mail server flaw that let attackers inject commands through its SNMP monitoring component.

d: Psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or revealing confidential information — exploiting human trust rather than technical vulnerabilities.
e: An attacker posed as a frantic executive and convinced an IT technician to reset credentials without proper verification.

d: SOCKS5 is a proxy protocol that forwards a user's network traffic through an intermediary machine, masking where the traffic really originates. Attackers hijack devices into SOCKS5 relays to anonymize their own activity behind someone else's IP address.
e: In August 2026, the Evooo1Bot Linux botnet turned infected routers into SOCKS5 relay nodes to launder criminal traffic.

d: The DoD system where contractors post their self-assessed NIST 800-171 score. During the CMMC pause, that self-reported number is the verification mechanism.
e: An inflated SPRS score is now the thing a prosecutor would cite, with no assessor standing in between.

d: An attack inserting malicious SQL code into a web form or URL to manipulate a database — commonly used to extract, modify, or delete data without authorization.
e: Attackers used SQL injection on a retail login page to bypass authentication and extract 2 million customer credit card numbers.

d: Compromising a supplier — a software library, an update mechanism, a service provider — so the compromise flows downstream to all their customers at once.
e: Hugging Face specifically confirmed its software supply chain was "verified clean," because a poisoned model repository would infect thousands of organizations.

d: When user-supplied text is fed into a template engine (which fills in placeholders like {{name}}) and the engine executes it as instructions rather than treating it as plain text.
e: Hugging Face's breach began with a template injection in a dataset configuration file uploaded by the attacker.

d: Any individual, group, or entity responsible for a cyberattack or security incident. Includes nation-states, organized crime groups, hacktivists, and malicious insiders.
e: The Lazarus Group, attributed to North Korea, has stolen over $3 billion in cryptocurrency to fund state activities.

d: A vendor-specific codename (UTA0533, APT29, Sandworm, Scattered Spider) for a cluster of related activity. Different vendors often use different names for the same group.
e: UTA0533 is Volexity's naming scheme; another firm may later reveal it overlaps with a group they already track.

d: The opening negotiation of an encrypted (HTTPS) connection, where client and server agree on keys before any real data flows. Handshake messages are processed before the server trusts you, so bugs there are reachable by anyone.
e: HollowByte abuses a length field in a TLS handshake message: OpenSSL believed the attacker's declared size and reserved up to 131 KB for a body that never arrived (July 2026).

d: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures — the behavior patterns and methods used by threat actors to plan, execute, and conceal cyberattacks. Understanding TTPs helps defenders anticipate attacks.
e: Analyzing a group's TTPs allowed defenders to block their attack before any data was exfiltrated.

d: Typosquatting is registering a package name, domain, or handle that looks almost identical to a trusted one, hoping people or automated tools pick the fake by mistake.
e: In August 2026, attackers poisoned the popular Rust arrayref crate by adding a dependency called 'proc-macro1', a typosquatting impersonation of the legitimate proc-macro2 package.

d: Same idea as pre-auth: the request carries no proof of identity. Any anonymous visitor qualifies.
e: Wp2shell works from an anonymous HTTP request to a WordPress site.

d: A memory-safety bug where a program keeps using a chunk of memory after it has already been released for reuse. Attackers can fill that freed space with their own data to crash the program or run their own code.
e: In July 2026, researchers used a use-after-free bug in Redis Streams to build a proof-of-concept that achieved remote code execution, prompting Redis to ship seven emergency releases.

d: A long unique number identifying a device or object. Fine as a label — dangerous when it is used as a secret, because identifiers are usually readable by anyone on the box.
e: SonicWall derived a service password from the appliance's product_uuid, a file any local user can read — so the identifier was effectively the password (July 2026).

d: Voice phishing: a scam carried out over a phone call in which the attacker impersonates a colleague, IT helpdesk, or trusted party to trick someone into revealing credentials or approving access.
e: In July 2026, the ShinyHunters extortion gang used Vishing to trick healthcare helpdesk staff into resetting passwords and changing MFA, then stole data from cloud platforms.

d: VoLTE (Voice over LTE) is the technology that carries phone calls as data over the 4G LTE network instead of over older circuit-switched voice systems, enabling higher-quality voice and video calls. Because it runs on the phone's modem software, bugs in that software can sometimes be triggered simply by placing a specially crafted call.
e: In August 2026, researchers showed a VoLTE video call could trigger an exploit chain giving full Android kernel access on phones using certain Unisoc chipsets.

d: Virtual Private Network — encrypts your internet connection and masks your IP address, creating a secure tunnel for data. Commonly used to secure remote work connections.
e: Attackers exploited an unpatched VPN vulnerability to gain internal network access without any employee credentials.

d: A weakness or flaw in software, hardware, or system design that could be exploited by attackers to gain unauthorized access or cause harm to a system.
e: A vulnerability in a popular PDF reader allowed code execution simply by opening a specially crafted PDF file.

d: A small malicious script uploaded to a compromised web server that gives an attacker a remote command-line-like interface, letting them keep control of the site even after the original flaw is patched.
e: After exploiting the 'wp2shell' WordPress flaw, attackers dropped a web shell to maintain access to the site.

d: WebSockets keep a two-way connection open between browser and server for live data. An attacker who can open one to an internal service turns it into a pipe from the internet straight to software that was only ever meant to be reachable from the machine itself.
e: CVE-2026-15409 let an unauthenticated /wsproxy request open a WebSocket to localhost-only services on SonicWall SMA appliances (July 2026).

d: Servers like nginx split work across several worker processes that each handle many connections. Crashing one drops every connection it was serving, so a crash bug in a worker is a real outage, not a hiccup.
e: CVE-2026-42533 overflows a buffer in an nginx worker process, crashing or restarting it and denying service to everyone it was handling (July 2026).

d: A security model that assumes no user, device or connection is trustworthy just because it is already inside the network. Every single request has to prove who it is and that it is allowed, every time, instead of being waved through after one login at the perimeter.
e: In July 2026, Senator Ron Wyden asked NIST to publish binding Zero Trust standards for federal agencies and give them two years to remove legacy VPN gateways, arguing that one breached edge device should not expose an entire agency network.

d: An attack that needs no action from the victim at all — not even a click. Just receiving, opening, or previewing a message can be enough to trigger it, which makes these attacks very hard to avoid through user caution alone.
e: In July 2026, Russia's Laundry Bear group used a zero-click flaw in Zimbra webmail (CVE-2025-66376) to steal 90 days of email the moment a victim merely previewed a booby-trapped message.

d: A vulnerability unknown to the software vendor with no available patch. Called zero-day because developers have had zero days to fix it — highly dangerous and valuable to attackers.
e: A nation-state used a zero-day in a widely-used VPN product to compromise government networks in five countries before the vendor knew the flaw existed.
